analyses.disclaimer: AI-generated STRIDE threat model. Each claim asserts that an attacker action against the named elements is credible against what the submitted text stated — never that a control is absent, and never that anything not listed here is safe. claims.title: Shared build token may be intercepted on the runner-to-controller crossing
claims.description: `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` crosses from the separate build environment to the corporate network, and its `encryption_in_transit` value is unknown. If that segment lacks effective transport encryption, an attacker able to observe the inter-zone path can intercept the shared build token used by `process:build-runner` to call `process:deploy-controller`, along with the selected image SHA. The disclosed, never-rotated credential enables subsequent access to the deploy-controller release-setting path and therefore supports attacks against releases consumed by the store estate; this threat concerns obtaining the credential, not altering a release.

grounds.text: The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline was set up.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release:encryption_in_transit`: an attacker must obtain an on-path position across the documented boundary crossing, but the static shared token makes capture immediately reusable. Impact is high because the disclosed credential authorizes the release-setting path of `process:deploy-controller`, whose chosen release is polled by the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt and mutually authenticate the release-setting flow
mitigations.detail: Require TLS 1.2+ with mTLS for `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, validating the deploy controller and build-runner identities across the boundary.

mitigations.summary: Replace the shared static build token
mitigations.detail: Issue a distinct, short-lived workload credential per pipeline, scope it only to the required release operation, and rotate the existing shared token.

claims.title: Shared build token leaves release changes unattributable to a specific pipeline
claims.description: A holder of the shared credential can set a new current release through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` at `process:deploy-controller` and later deny having done so. The flow's token is stated to be the same for every pipeline, so a record naming that token or the build runner can narrow a disputed release change only to the population of pipeline holders, not establish which pipeline or actor selected the image SHA. A disputed change to the deployment record then propagates when `process:store-server` polls the controller and pulls the selected image across the estate; accountability for a release affecting approximately 1,200 stores collapses even if the controller retains an event record.

grounds.text: The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: exploiting the gap requires access to a pipeline that can present the shared token, but `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` crosses from `boundary:build-environment` into `boundary:corporate-network` and the shared credential cannot distinguish its holders. Impact is high: `process:deploy-controller` holds `business-critical-data`, and its release choice is consumed by `process:store-server` across the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Use a distinct, attributable deployment identity per pipeline
mitigations.detail: Replace the shared token on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` with short-lived per-pipeline credentials and retain the verified pipeline and initiating-user identity with each release-change event.

mitigations.summary: Record an immutable release-change trail
mitigations.detail: Have `process:deploy-controller` emit structured, append-only audit events containing the prior and new image SHA, verified principal, originating build identifier, timestamp, and outcome.

claims.title: Manual rebuilds may not be attributable to the developer who triggered them
claims.description: A developer can trigger an unreviewed rebuild of main through `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` and later deny having initiated it. That flow crosses from the inferred `boundary:corporate-network` location of `entity:developer` into `boundary:build-environment`, but its `authentication` is unknown. If the unknown authentication does not establish and retain an individual verified principal, neither the rebuild nor the resulting image pushed by `process:build-runner` can be rebuttably tied to the developer who initiated it. The resulting deployment can reach `process:deploy-controller` and then every `process:store-server`; this claim is conditional on the unresolved authentication attribute, not an assertion that no individual authentication or audit record exists.

grounds.text: any developer can log in to the build runner and kick off a rebuild of `main` by hand; that path does not require a merge and is not reviewed

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `authentication` on `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild:authentication`: a developer must access the internal rebuild path, but the path is available to any developer and crosses into the build environment. Impact is high: `process:build-runner` handles `credentials` and `business-critical-data`, and a rebuild can produce an image that is selected by the deploy controller for the store estate.

mitigations.summary: Require and preserve individual identity for manual rebuilds
mitigations.detail: Use individual, non-shared authentication on `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` and log the verified developer identity, source, requested ref, build ID, timestamp, and result in a protected audit trail.

mitigations.summary: Bind deployments to reviewed build provenance
mitigations.detail: Require the deploy path to retain the initiating identity and immutable build provenance from `process:build-runner` through the release update, so a manual rebuild cannot be indistinguishable from an approved main-branch build.

claims.title: Counterfeit dependencies can impersonate the public package registry to the build runner
claims.description: An attacker able to substitute a response on the internet-facing dependency path can impersonate `entity:public-package-registry` to `process:build-runner` over `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`. The runner explicitly does not verify package signatures, so it accepts a counterfeit package as the named registry dependency. Second-order: the runner incorporates that code into an image, which can be pushed to `store:image-registry`, selected through `process:deploy-controller`, and pulled by the fleet represented by `process:store-server`.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies` crosses from `boundary:build-environment` to `boundary:internet` and explicitly lacks package-signature authentication; impact is high because compromised build content can propagate through `store:image-registry` and `process:deploy-controller` to the approximately 1,200 `availability-critical` `process:store-server` instances.

mitigations.summary: Verify signed dependency provenance before building
mitigations.detail: Require `process:build-runner` to verify signatures and trusted publisher identity for every package obtained through `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, rejecting unsigned or untrusted artifacts.

mitigations.summary: Make transport authentication explicit for registry resolution
mitigations.detail: Use TLS with full certificate-chain validation and document `encryption_in_transit` and endpoint verification for the public-registry flow, reducing opportunities to substitute registry responses.

claims.title: A shared build token can be used to impersonate the build runner to the deploy controller
claims.description: An attacker who obtains the shared build token can present it on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` and act as `process:build-runner` to `process:deploy-controller`. Because the token is the same for every pipeline and has never been rotated, it does not provide a distinct, revocable workload identity. Second-order: the impersonator can select the image sha the estate should run, causing `process:store-server` instances to poll the controller and deploy the selected release across the store fleet.

Impact is high because `process:deploy-controller` controls the release selected by approximately 1,200 `process:store-server` instances, which are tagged `availability-critical` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Replace the shared token with per-workload short-lived identity
mitigations.detail: Authenticate `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` using a unique workload identity such as mTLS or short-lived audience-bound tokens, so each pipeline is independently attributable and revocable.

mitigations.detail: Until workload identity is deployed, rotate the shared token, store it in an appropriate secret-management mechanism, and restrict it to only the release-selection operation required by `process:build-runner`.

claims.title: Unsigned public dependency can be planted into released till images
claims.description: An attacker able to publish a substituted dependency at `entity:public-package-registry` can plant it through `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, because the build runner does not verify package signatures. `process:build-runner` incorporates the dependency into the container image it produces. Second-order, the image is published to `store:image-registry`, selected as a release, and pulled and restarted by the store-server fleet, turning a package substitution into altered till-software behavior.

Impact is high: `process:build-runner` produces release images, and altered till software can reach the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Verify signed, immutable dependency artifacts
mitigations.detail: Require `process:build-runner` to verify package signatures against trusted publisher keys and enforce lockfile hashes before accepting packages from `entity:public-package-registry`.

mitigations.summary: Protect dependency retrieval in transit
mitigations.detail: Use authenticated TLS with certificate validation on `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, while retaining signature verification as an end-to-end integrity control.

Second-order, the runner packages the altered code into an image in `store:image-registry`; once selected as the current release, store servers can deploy the altered till software. claims.title: Repeated manual rebuilds can exhaust build-runner capacity and block releases
claims.description: A malicious or compromised `entity:developer` on the corporate network can repeatedly invoke `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, which permits any developer to trigger a rebuild of main without a merge. Each rebuild makes `process:build-runner` fetch source, resolve dependencies, build an image, and push it to `store:image-registry`; repeated requests can consume its finite build CPU, memory, worker slots, dependency-download capacity, or registry throughput faster than a developer spends to submit them. The source disclosure enables targeted attacks on `process:build-runner` and downstream release artifacts. This is conditional on the unknown encryption-at-rest value; it does not assert that the git server is unencrypted.

grounds.text: Developers push their branches to our self-hosted git server
Nobody has documented whether the git server encrypts what it stores

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_at_rest` on `store:git-server`, `data_classification` on `store:git-server`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:store:git-server:encryption_at_rest`: obtaining an operational storage copy requires storage-layer access, but the model verifies no encryption-at-rest control. Impact is medium because `store:git-server` contains the source that feeds the build runner and is tagged business-critical-data, making disclosure useful for targeted follow-on attacks.

mitigations.summary: Establish and enforce encrypted git storage
mitigations.detail: Determine the at-rest posture of `store:git-server`, then require managed-key encryption for its primary volumes, backups, snapshots, replicas, and decommissioned media.

mitigations.summary: Constrain access to repository copies
mitigations.detail: Separate backup and storage-administration principals from repository readers, restrict export permissions, and audit snapshot and backup access.

claims.title: Image-registry operational copies may expose deployed software if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:image-registry` retains commit-tagged container images, but its `encryption_at_rest` and `data_classification` attributes are unknown. If storage encryption is absent, someone obtaining an image-registry backup, snapshot, volume, or other storage-layer copy can read the images without authenticating as a store server. The recovered artifacts disclose the till software distributed to `process:store-server` and enable tailored follow-on attacks against the fleet. This is a conditional finding about the unresolved encryption-at-rest attribute, not an assertion that the registry is unencrypted.

grounds.text: It pushes the finished image to our image registry, which is also in the build environment. Images are tagged with the commit sha.
Nobody has documented whether the git server encrypts what it stores, or whether the image registry does.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_at_rest` on `store:image-registry`, `data_classification` on `store:image-registry`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:store:image-registry:encryption_at_rest`: storage-layer access is required, but encryption is unverified. Impact is medium because `store:image-registry` holds business-critical deployment images that are pulled and executed by store servers across the estate.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt registry data and all operational copies
mitigations.detail: Establish whether `store:image-registry` is encrypted at rest, then enforce managed-key encryption for registry storage, backups, snapshots, replicas, and retired volumes.

mitigations.summary: Limit and monitor artifact export access
mitigations.detail: Use least-privilege registry and storage permissions, separate backup-reader roles from store pull roles, and log or alert on image and snapshot exports.

claims.title: A counterfeit image registry could be accepted by store servers if registry authentication is absent
claims.description: `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` crosses from `boundary:store-estate` to `boundary:build-environment`, but both its `authentication` and `encryption_in_transit` attributes are unknown. If those unknowns resolve to no verified registry server identity and certificate validation, an attacker with a position on the retail WAN could impersonate `store:image-registry` to `process:store-server` and provide a counterfeit image for the requested release. Second-order: each affected store server restarts the container it pulls, so one successful registry impersonation can affect the fleet represented by `process:store-server`. This draft is conditional on the undocumented authentication and transport controls; it does not assert that they are absent.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `authentication` on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`, `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because the store-to-registry flow crosses the retail WAN but exploitation requires an attacker to obtain an on-path or endpoint-substitution position; the relevant authentication and transit-encryption controls are undocumented. Impact is high because a counterfeit image would be restarted by the approximately 1,200 servers represented by `process:store-server`, which is tagged `availability-critical` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Require authenticated TLS for image pulls
mitigations.detail: Set explicit transport protection for `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`: use TLS 1.2+ with full certificate-chain validation and constrain registry certificate issuance through a private CA or workload identity.

mitigations.summary: Verify image provenance before restart
mitigations.detail: Require `process:store-server` to verify signed image provenance and an expected immutable digest before accepting content from `store:image-registry`, so a substituted registry endpoint cannot supply a trusted-looking image.

claims.title: Flooding the shared deploy controller can prevent estate-wide release polling
claims.description: `process:deploy-controller` is a shared chokepoint: every `process:store-server` polls it over `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release` once per minute to learn the current image sha. If an attacker with a foothold in `boundary:store-estate` floods that cross-boundary flow, or if the flow's `authentication: unknown` resolves to insufficient caller admission, the attacker can exhaust the controller's request-handling capacity with cheap polling requests. The model states no per-store request cap, timeout, backoff, or degradation behavior. Second-order, legitimate polling by the roughly 1,200 store servers fails or queues behind the flood, so the estate cannot learn or retrieve an intended release from `store:image-registry`; recovery or urgent deployment is delayed across all stores.

grounds.text: We run about 1,200 stores.
Every store server asks the deploy controller once a minute what the current release is

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `authentication` on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`, `protocol` on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low because the attacker needs a foothold in `boundary:store-estate` or the unresolved admission weakness on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`; the flow's authentication and protocol are both `unknown`. Impact is medium because the shared `process:deploy-controller` serves about 1,200 `process:store-server` instances, so a successful flood blocks estate-wide release polling and emergency deployment, but the model does not state that stores cease running their current till containers when polling fails.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate and rate-bound each store poller
mitigations.detail: Establish and enforce a distinct authenticated identity for each `process:store-server` on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`, with per-store request ceilings and rejection of unauthenticated callers.

mitigations.summary: Prevent polling failures from becoming a controller-wide outage
mitigations.detail: Set short request timeouts, bounded queues, exponential backoff with jitter, and circuit breakers at `process:store-server` and `process:deploy-controller` so overload fails fast instead of accumulating concurrent polls.

rejected_claims.title: Unsigned public dependencies can execute with build-runner deployment authority
rejected_claims.description: An attacker who can cause `entity:public-package-registry` to return a malicious package named by the lockfile can have that package execute while `process:build-runner` resolves dependencies over `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`. The runner does not verify package signatures, so supplied dependency logic inherits the runner's authority rather than the authority of the public source. This escalates an internet-originating package-supply position into the shared build token's authority on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`: the attacker can produce and publish a malicious image, select it as the current release, and ultimately obtain code execution on the `process:store-server` fleet when servers pull and restart that image.

grounds.text: the lockfile is taken as given — the runner does not verify signatures on what it downloads
The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline was set up.

verdict.reason: The model states that the runner resolves and incorporates lockfile dependencies, but it does not state that a downloaded dependency executes within `process:build-runner` during resolution or otherwise obtains the runner's deployment-token authority.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies` crosses to the internet and has stated-absent package authentication, but exploitation requires an attacker to control or substitute a dependency response. Impact is high: `process:build-runner` can set releases through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, and the resulting image is pulled and restarted by the availability-critical `process:store-server` fleet.

mitigations.summary: Require verified, immutable build dependencies
mitigations.detail: Configure `process:build-runner` to accept only dependencies whose signatures and trusted publisher identities are verified, and resolve from immutable package digests or an internally controlled repository.

mitigations.summary: Isolate dependency execution from deployment authority
mitigations.detail: Resolve and build untrusted dependency content in a sandboxed workload without the shared deployment token; require a separate, narrowly scoped and short-lived identity for `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`.
